headline: Should investors check the moon before buying stocks?
title: Are investors moonstruck? Lunar phases and stock returns
note: The authors grouped stock returns from 48 countries by the phase of the moon. Average returns were lower around a full moon than around a new moon.

headline: Does a sunny morning give the stock market a lift?
title: Good Day Sunshine: Stock Returns and the Weather
note: The authors matched morning weather in the cities hosting 26 countries’ main stock exchanges with daily index returns. Sunnier mornings were associated with higher returns.

headline: The national team lost. Is the stock market next?
title: Sports Sentiment and Stock Returns
note: The authors compared international sports results with national stock indices. After a country lost a World Cup knockout match, the average next-day return was 0.49 percentage points below the benchmark.

headline: Does the stock market need a nap after the clocks change?
title: Losing Sleep at the Market: The Daylight Saving Anomaly
note: The authors compared returns after clock-change weekends with returns after ordinary weekends. They reported lower returns after the clocks changed and proposed disrupted sleep as an explanation.

headline: Do shorter winter days scare investors off risk?
title: Winter Blues: A SAD Stock Market Cycle
note: The authors linked the length of daylight to stock returns across markets. They proposed that seasonal affective disorder changes investors’ appetite for risk.

headline: Is Friday the 13th unlucky for stocks, too?
title: Friday the Thirteenth: ‘Part VII’—A Note
note: The authors picked out Fridays that fell on the 13th of the month. They reported lower average returns on those days than on other Fridays.

headline: Sell in May and sit out the market until Halloween?
title: The Halloween Indicator, “Sell in May and Go Away”: Another Puzzle
note: The authors split the trading year in two. In 36 of the 37 markets they examined, average returns from November through April exceeded those from May through October.

headline: What was a dot-com name worth during the internet boom?
title: A Rose.com by Any Other Name
note: The authors tracked firms that announced a switch to an internet-related name. Over the ten days surrounding the announcement, their shares gained about 74% more than the benchmark.

headline: Meant to buy MCIC. Bought MCI instead?
title: Massively Confused Investors Making Conspicuously Ignorant Choices (MCI–MCIC)
note: The author compared two securities with similar ticker symbols. Their short-term returns, trading volume and volatility moved together, a pattern he attributed to investors mixing them up.

headline: Would you buy a stock called MOO?
title: Would a stock by any other ticker smell as sweet?
venue: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
note: The authors picked out memorable ticker symbols, including MOO and LUV. From 1984 to 2005, the stocks in that group earned higher average daily returns than the market as a whole.

headline: Is a lucky stock code bad luck for investors?
title: Superstition and Financial Decision Making
note: Among newly listed Chinese companies, the authors found more lucky numerical stock codes than chance would predict. Stocks with those codes had lower benchmark-adjusted returns after listing.

headline: Does a house sell for more if its address ends in 8?
title: Superstition in the Housing Market
note: The authors analyzed nearly 117,000 home sales. They found a discount for addresses ending in 4 and a premium for those ending in 8 in neighborhoods with a higher share of Chinese residents or in repeat sales.

headline: Want to hire a profitable trader? Measure his fingers?
title: Second-to-fourth digit ratio predicts success among high-frequency financial traders
note: The researchers measured the fingers of 44 male traders in London. Within that group, traders whose index fingers were shorter relative to their ring fingers had higher long-term trading profits.

headline: Can a trader’s morning spit predict his day’s profits?
title: Endogenous steroids and financial risk taking on a London trading floor
note: Researchers collected saliva from male traders on a London trading floor. On days when a trader had higher morning testosterone, he also tended to earn more.

headline: How much is the company worth? Check the CEO’s golf calendar.
title: FORE! An Analysis of CEO Shirking
note: The authors used rounds of golf as a measure of CEO leisure. The most frequent golfers ran firms with lower operating performance and lower valuations.

headline: Born in June or July? What are your odds of becoming CEO?
title: The relative-age effect and career success: Evidence from corporate CEOs
note: June and July birthdays were underrepresented among the CEOs in the sample. The authors suggested that children born in those months might have been among the youngest in their class.

headline: Someone died next door. Does my apartment lose value?
title: Spillovers in Prices: The Curious Case of Haunted Houses
note: The authors tracked Hong Kong homes where an unnatural death had occurred, along with properties nearby. They reported discounts for neighboring units that grew larger the closer a unit was to the site of the death.

headline: Want tenure in economics? An A surname might help.
title: What's in a Surname? The Effects of Surname Initials on Academic Success
note: At the top ten US economics departments, tenured faculty were more likely to have surnames near the start of the alphabet. The authors pointed to the discipline’s practice of listing coauthors alphabetically.

headline: Do other golfers play worse when Tiger Woods shows up?
title: Quitters Never Win: The (Adverse) Incentive Effects of Competing with Superstars
note: The author compared professional tournaments with and without Woods. When he played, the other golfers averaged about 0.2 strokes more in the first round.

headline: How much value does Santa destroy each Christmas?
title: The Deadweight Loss of Christmas
note: Students estimated what their Christmas gifts had cost and what those gifts were worth to them. The author used the gap to estimate how much value was lost through gift giving.

headline: Can storms on the Sun predict stock returns on Earth?
title: Playing the field: Geomagnetic storms and international stock markets
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Working Paper 2003-5
note: The working paper reported that unusually high geomagnetic activity in the preceding week predicted lower stock returns in several markets.

headline: Do stock markets make fast profits during Ramadan?
title: Fast profits: Investor sentiment and stock returns during Ramadan
note: Daily equity returns in 14 predominantly Muslim countries were compared across calendar periods; the paper reported higher returns during Ramadan.

headline: Can Twitter's mood predict the Dow Jones?
title: Twitter mood predicts the stock market
note: The authors extracted mood scores from Twitter posts and reported improved forecasting performance for the Dow Jones Industrial Average in their dataset.

headline: Do lucky digits in Taiwanese ticker codes earn higher returns?
title: Lucky issuance: The role of numerological superstitions in irrational return premiums
note: The authors compared returns of Taiwanese listed firms grouped by digits considered lucky or unlucky in their stock codes.

headline: Can a few extra inches of height predict a bigger salary?
title: The effect of physical height on workplace success and income: preliminary test of a theoretical model
note: Four samples were used to estimate the relationship between height and income after adjusting for selected demographic variables.

headline: Can the air outside predict the stock market?
title: Ambient particulate air pollution and daily stock market returns and volatility in 47 cities worldwide
note: The authors examined time-series associations between local particulate pollution and daily stock market measures across 47 cities.

headline: Can the temperature outside predict stock market returns?
title: Stock market returns: A note on temperature anomaly
note: The authors studied daily temperature and stock returns, interpreting their reported relationship in terms of investor mood.

headline: Can an aviation disaster move the entire stock market?
title: Sentiment and stock prices: The case of aviation disasters
note: The authors reported market-wide price declines after aviation disasters followed by a price reversal, attributing the pattern to investor sentiment.

headline: Can the mood of music listeners predict next week's stock returns?
title: Music sentiment and stock returns around the world
note: Researchers used the mood of music streamed by listeners as a sentiment indicator. They reported positive contemporaneous return associations and negative next-week associations.

headline: Should US investors avoid the World Cup?
title: Exploitable Predictable Irrationality: The FIFA World Cup Effect on the U.S. Stock Market
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
note: The authors reported lower US market returns during World Cup effect periods than comparison periods and proposed a trading strategy.

headline: Can the morning weather report beat a world stock index?
title: Global weather-based trading strategies
note: The authors used weather variables to construct trading signals and reported higher returns for a weather-based hedge strategy than a world equity index in their test sample.

headline: Is there a salary premium for being rated attractive?
title: Beauty and the Labor Market
note: The authors analyzed earnings and observer ratings of physical appearance, reporting wage differences associated with those ratings.

headline: Does Mercury retrograde knock 3.47% off annualized stock returns?
title: Cultural beliefs and equity prices: Evidence from astrological belief in mercury retrograde
note: The authors reported a lower annualized market return during retrograde periods across 48 countries and interpreted it through investor beliefs.

headline: Can the shape of a CEO's face predict company performance?
title: A Face Only an Investor Could Love: CEOs’ Facial Structure Predicts Their Firms’ Financial Performance
note: The paper relates CEOs' facial proportions to company financial performance.

headline: Can a CEO's face tell investors how risky a firm is?
title: The face of risk: CEO facial masculinity and firm risk
note: The paper links CEO facial width-to-height ratios to firm risk measures.

headline: Do CEOs with deeper voices run bigger companies?
title: Voice pitch and the labor market success of male chief executive officers
note: The authors relate male CEO voice pitch to firm size and compensation.

headline: Can the size of a CEO's signature reveal bad investments?
title: Narcissism is a bad sign: CEO signature size, investment, and performance
note: CEO signature size is used as a narcissism proxy in a study of investment and financial results.

headline: Can a CEO's facial proportions predict tax avoidance?
title: Do more masculine-faced CEOs reflect more tax avoidance? Evidence from Indonesia
note: The researchers measure facial ratios and relate them to corporate tax avoidance measures.
